content: The values and preferences of individuals regarding decentralization, task-shifting, and integration of hepatitis C virus (HCV) services among potential end users are critical to consider. Despite significant advancements in the quality and affordability of HCV treatment in recent years, the service delivery pathway remains particularly burdensome for many individuals exposed to or living with HCV. Marginalized communities are disproportionately affected by HCV and often face additional barriers such as stigma and discrimination. Therefore, it is essential to identify the specific values and preferences of people living with HCV or those at risk of exposure to propose services tailored to their needs. An anonymous, self-administered online survey was conducted in English to gather insights. The survey was developed collaboratively by the World Hepatitis Alliance, Coalition PLUS, and the World Health Organization (WHO). It consisted of 42 multiple-choice questions with an option to provide additional information. Participants were required to be 18 years or older, living with or affected by HCV, and willing to participate. The survey was promoted through social media, mailing lists, and direct contacts by Coalition PLUS, the World Hepatitis Alliance, regional WHO offices, and the Treatment Action Group. Data collection occurred between September 8 and September 22, 2021. A total of 210 individuals from 49 countries participated in the survey. The median age of participants was 42 years (IQR: 33–52). The majority were male (56%, n=113), followed by females (40%, n=81), transgender individuals (1%, n=2), and gender non-binary individuals (2%, n=4). Most participants reported living in urban or large city areas (69%, n=137) and had completed tertiary education (88%, n=175). Among the participants, 72% (n=150) had previously been tested for HCV, with 40% (n=60) testing positive. Of the 56 respondents who provided information on HCV treatment, 91% (n=51) were either currently undergoing or had completed treatment. Participants identified with various groups, including 23% living with HCV, 18% who inject drugs, 21% who formerly injected drugs, and 16% living with HIV. Regarding preferred testing locations, 45% preferred community-based organizations, and 44% preferred primary care clinics. A significant majority (88%) expressed a preference for conducting both initial and confirmatory tests on the same day, citing faster status confirmation (81%) and quicker treatment initiation (76%) as the main reasons. Additionally, 93% preferred to conduct both tests at the same location, emphasizing convenience (70%) and a community-friendly environment (60%). Participants also expressed strong preferences for treatment locations that were free from discrimination and where they felt comfortable. For example, one participant from the UK who identified as a person who injects drugs stated, It needs to be somewhere that I feel comfortable and not face negative attitudes. Similarly, 85% of participants indicated they would like to start treatment on the same day if they tested positive for HCV, with reasons including avoiding exposing family and friends to HCV (28%) and ensuring continued follow-up from testing to treatment (27%). Furthermore, 92% preferred to be tested and treated in the same location, citing convenience (34%) and continuity of care (32%). Decentralized services were found to be particularly advantageous for both testing and treatment. A culturally competent approach was deemed essential for testing and treatment services. Strong preferences were observed for same-day testing and treatment at the same location, which could potentially improve linkage to care. Offering a range of HCV testing and treatment solutions would be beneficial to address the diverse needs of different populations and situations. In Malaysia, the HCV treatment decentralization model has demonstrated success. The introduction of simplified care pathways, task-shifting to nurses, and integration of HCV services into primary healthcare settings has proven feasible and cost-effective. Simplified and decentralized HCV services are crucial for scaling up care and treatment, regardless of a country’s income classification. For example, nurse-led pilot projects in rural areas have shown that task-shifting does not compromise treatment safety or efficacy. In these pilots, nurses initiated direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy for uncomplicated cases, achieving a sustained virologic response (SVR) rate of 98%. Despite challenges such as limited access to diagnostic tools and a shortage of hepatologists, the implementation of decentralized and simplified HCV care pathways has been effective. Active case finding in local villages and passive case finding in rural health centers have been employed to identify patients. Simplified training programs for nurses, general practitioners, and laboratory technicians have supported the expansion of HCV services. These efforts have resulted in high cure rates and improved patient outcomes, demonstrating the feasibility and effectiveness of decentralized HCV care models.
